variants.prompt: For Bare-metal cycle and timer measurement: 1. Read the exact DDI0403E.e DEMCR/DWT scopes and selected-device/core identity. DEMCR at 0xE000EDFC has TRCENA bit 24; DWT_CTRL at 0xE0001000 has NOCYCCNT bit 25/CYCCNTENA bit 0; CYCCNT is at 0xE0001004. Access through the already accepted implementation's MMIO contract. Presence/access/errata/clock are implementation checks, not assumptions from these addresses. Predict normal, boundary and failure outcomes before running the code. Reject an out-of-width endpoint, nonboolean feature flag, unknown clock or bound admitting a full wrap. The core counter is optional and may be inaccessible; those results must not become zero cycles. Debug state stops CYCCNT, so a halted span cannot be converted into full wall elapsed time. An overhead subtraction at or below overhead is inconclusive. Interrupt cycles, clock changes and probe effects remain in scope unless independently controlled.

sets.title: Merkle commitments and bounded anti-entropy

objective_text.T76.07.a: Derive a domain-separated Merkle root for an exact ordered leaf sequence, distinguishing hash equality under a collision assumption from identity authentication, availability or a proof that arbitrary bytes are well formed.
objective_text.T76.07.b: Derive padding across55/56/63/64/65-byte boundaries, uint32 modular arithmetic, round constants and endian conversion. Prove the tree shape for non-power-of-two counts and that a subtree comparison is meaningful only with the same position/range/domain. Account for hash collision and corrupt-peer assumptions; a matching root alone authenticates no sender and guarantees no retrievability.
objective_text.T76.07.c: Run replicated.merkle, standard empty/abc hash vectors, all padding boundaries and independent randomized hashlib differential cases. Kill omitted leaf-domain prefix and ignored right-child mutants. Inspect the generated code for the intended unsigned operations; benchmark nodes hashed versus full leaf comparison under equal correctness/security contracts.
objective_text.T76.07.d: Add inclusion proofs with explicit leaf index/count, verify malformed/truncated/extra paths, then implement anti-entropy over a synthetic local framed transport. Vary chunking and domain identifiers and show root incompatibility. Model a malicious peer returning a missing or inconsistent node; fail without publishing partial repaired state. Do not claim collision resistance from a finite test suite.

objective_text.T76.09.a: Implement the T20.03 functional-core boundary: explicit state and recorded input produce new state and effect requests, while an adapter owns effects. Demonstrate rollback equivalence without replaying externally visible effects or claiming that ordinary C enforces purity.
objective_text.T76.09.b: Prove determinism from complete state/input and defined unsigned arithmetic. Identify every effect boundary and distinguish speculative requests from committed presentation. sets.title: T09 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define archive, weak symbol, shared object, dynamic loader, global offset table and load address (LMA) without the glossary and name the source for each.
checklist: archive: A static library: an ar collection of object files with a symbol index from which the linker extracts only the members that resolve currently undefined symbols, in the order the archives appear on the command line; a member needed by a later object is not pulled in unless the archive is repeated or grouped.

dynamic loader: The program interpreter (ld.so) named in a dynamically linked executable's PT_INTERP segment, which the kernel starts first; it maps the needed shared objects in search order, applies dynamic relocations and then jumps to the executable's entry point.

entry symbol: The symbol the linker records as the program's entry point (ENTRY in a linker script, -e on the command line), which for a hosted program is _start and for Cortex-M firmware is irrelevant because the vector table, not the ELF header, selects the reset handler.

global offset table: A per-object table of addresses filled by the loader so that position-independent code can reach global data and functions indirectly; the procedure linkage table pairs with it for lazy function binding.

link order: The rule that the linker resolves undefined symbols from inputs left to right, extracting archive members only for symbols undefined at the moment the archive is scanned; the reason an unresolved symbol can be fixed by reordering rather than by adding code.

load address: The address at which a section's bytes are placed in the image (LMA), as opposed to the address at which the code expects to find them at run time (VMA); when they differ, as for .data in flash, startup code must copy the section from LMA to VMA before main.

map file: The linker's report of where every input section and symbol landed, which archive members were pulled in and why, and how much of each memory region is used; the first place to look for an unexpected size or a missing section.

orphan section: An input section that no SECTIONS rule of the linker script places, which the linker drops into an output section of its own choosing; in firmware it can land outside flash or at the wrong alignment, so scripts should either name every section or make orphans an error.

relocatable link: A link (-r) whose output is another relocatable object file combining the inputs without resolving external references or assigning final addresses; used to build incremental objects or to apply a linker script fragment before the final link.

RELRO: Relocation read-only: a linker arrangement (-z relro, full with -z now) that places relocated data such as the global offset table in a segment the loader marks read-only after binding, removing it as an overwrite target.

section garbage collection: The linker's removal of unreferenced input sections (--gc-sections with per-function sections) to shrink an image; anything reached only through the vector table or by hardware must be protected with KEEP or it silently disappears.

shared object: An ELF file built from position-independent code that the dynamic loader maps into a process at run time and binds through dynamic symbol resolution; it shares code pages across processes and defines an ABI boundary that must stay compatible across versions.

stripping: Removing the symbol table, debug information and other non-loadable sections from an ELF file to shrink it; loadable segments are unaffected, so a stripped binary runs identically but backtraces and symbolic debugging need the separately kept debug file.

symbol versioning: The ELF mechanism by which a shared object exports several versions of one symbol (memcpy@GLIBC_2.14) so that old programs keep the behavior they were linked against; the reason a binary built against a newer glibc may refuse to load on an older one.

TLS segment (ELF): The PT_TLS program header describing the initialization image for thread-local storage, which the loader and libc copy for each thread and address through the thread pointer; the toolchain realization of the C thread storage duration.

weak symbol: A symbol with weak binding that a global definition of the same name overrides without a duplicate-definition error and that resolves to zero (or a null pointer) if nothing defines it; a toolchain feature with no ISO C counterpart, used for default handlers in vector tables.

sets.title: T23 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define process, file descriptor, open file description, zombie process, memory mapping and durability boundary without the glossary, naming the man page or POSIX section that defines each.
checklist: close-on-exec: A descriptor flag (FD_CLOEXEC, set atomically with O_CLOEXEC or SOCK_CLOEXEC) that makes the kernel close the descriptor during exec, preventing leaks of files and sockets into child programs; the flag belongs to the descriptor, not the open file description.

exec: Replacing the calling process's program image with a new one while keeping the process identity, open descriptors (unless close-on-exec), working directory and signal mask; a successful exec never returns.

file locking: Advisory record locks (fcntl F_SETLK) or whole-file locks (flock) that cooperating processes consult before accessing a file; advisory means the kernel does not stop a process that ignores them, and the two lock families do not see each other.

file offset: The position in a file at which the next read or write occurs, stored in the open file description and therefore shared by every descriptor duplicated from the same open; pread and pwrite take an explicit offset and leave it unchanged.

fork: The system call that creates a child process as a copy of the caller: same code, copy-on-write memory, duplicated descriptors sharing the parent's open file descriptions, and a return value that is 0 in the child and the child's process ID in the parent.

interrupted system call: A blocking call that returns -1 with errno set to EINTR because a signal handler ran; the operation did not complete and must be retried, unless the handler was installed with SA_RESTART and the call is one the kernel restarts automatically.

memory mapping: Making a region of a file, or anonymous zero-filled memory, appear in the address space with mmap, so that loads and stores replace read and write; a shared mapping writes through to the file and to other processes, a private mapping is copy-on-write.
orphan process: A process whose parent has terminated before it; the kernel re-parents it to init or a subreaper, which will reap it when it terminates.

pipe: A unidirectional byte-stream channel with a bounded kernel buffer, exposed as a read descriptor and a write descriptor; writes of at most PIPE_BUF bytes are atomic, reads return whatever is available, and a read on a pipe with no writers returns end of file.
reaping: Collecting a terminated child's exit status with wait or waitpid, which releases its process-table entry; until reaped, the terminated child remains a zombie.

redirection: Making a standard descriptor refer to a different open file description, done with dup2 before exec so that the child program reads or writes a file or pipe without knowing it; the shell's < and > operators do exactly this.

rename-based update: Replacing a file's contents atomically by writing a temporary file in the same directory, fsyncing it, renaming it over the target and fsyncing the directory; readers see either the old or the new file, never a mixture.

resource limit: A per-process soft and hard ceiling (RLIMIT_NOFILE, RLIMIT_STACK, RLIMIT_AS and others) enforced by the kernel; exceeding one turns a normally successful call into an error such as EMFILE, which robust programs must handle.

shared memory: Physical pages mapped into more than one address space, created with a shared file mapping, shm_open or anonymous shared mappings inherited across fork; the fastest IPC and the only one that reintroduces the memory model across processes.

virtual memory: The per-process address space the processor translates through page tables, letting the kernel map, protect, share and lazily back pages; the virtual size of a process says nothing about the physical memory it is using (its resident set).

sets.title: T25 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Without opening the glossary, define mutex, condition variable, spurious wakeup, publication (memory ordering) and false sharing in one sentence each, naming the normative source for each.
checklist: bounded queue: A producer/consumer channel with a fixed capacity that blocks or rejects producers when full and consumers when empty; capacity is the backpressure mechanism that keeps memory use and latency bounded under overload.

cache line: The unit of transfer and coherence between a cache and memory, typically 64 bytes on x86-64 and 32 bytes on Cortex-M7; alignment of hot data to lines and ownership of whole lines by DMA buffers are decided at this granularity.

compare-and-exchange: The atomic read-modify-write that stores a new value only if the object still holds the expected value, returning whether it did and updating the expected value otherwise; the weak form may fail spuriously and belongs in loops, the strong form does not.

compiler barrier: A construct such as an asm volatile statement with a memory clobber that forbids the compiler from moving memory accesses across it, without emitting any instruction; it constrains code generation only and gives no ordering guarantee to other processors or devices.

condition variable: A waiting primitive, always paired with a mutex, that lets a thread sleep until another thread signals that a predicate over shared state may have changed; the predicate is rechecked in a loop because wakeups can be spurious or stale.

deadlock: A state in which each thread of a set waits for a resource held by another thread of the set, so none can proceed; it requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait, and a global lock order removes the last condition.

false sharing: A performance defect in which independent variables used by different cores share a cache line, so each write invalidates the other core's copy; correct, race-free code can still be slowed by orders of magnitude until the variables are padded to separate lines.

hardware barrier: A processor instruction (DMB, DSB, ISB on Arm; MFENCE on x86-64) that constrains the order in which the processor's memory accesses become visible or complete; the implementation's tool for realizing fences and release/acquire semantics.

livelock: A failure of progress in which threads repeatedly react to one another (retrying, backing off, yielding) without any of them completing; lock-free retry loops and overly polite collision avoidance both produce it.
mutex: A mutual-exclusion lock that at most one thread holds at a time; unlocking it synchronizes with the next lock, so the critical section's writes happen before the next holder's reads

priority inversion: The situation in which a high-priority thread waits for a lock held by a low-priority thread that a medium-priority thread keeps preempting, so the effective priority order is inverted; priority inheritance or ceiling protocols bound it.

publication (memory ordering): Making data written by one thread visible to another by a release operation on a flag or pointer that the reader acquires: the writes before the release happen before everything after the matching acquire

read-write lock: A lock that admits any number of concurrent readers or exactly one writer; it pays off only when read sections are long and frequent, because the extra bookkeeping and writer starvation policy cost more than a plain mutex on short sections.

release sequence: The release operation on an atomic object together with the subsequent read-modify-write operations on it; an acquire that reads any value written by the sequence synchronizes with the head release, which is what makes reference counting with fetch_add correct.

semaphore: A counter with atomic wait (decrement or block when zero) and post (increment and wake) operations; it has no owner, so it can signal across contexts, including from an interrupt handler to a thread, where a mutex cannot be used.

spurious wakeup: A return from a condition-variable wait that no signal caused, which POSIX permits for efficiency; correct code therefore re-evaluates its predicate after every wakeup rather than assuming the condition holds.

starvation: The indefinite postponement of one thread while others keep making progress, caused by unfair scheduling, lock hand-off policy or priorities; fairness is the property that bounds how long any thread can be bypassed.

thread pool: A fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a bounded queue, bounding concurrency and thread-creation cost; its design questions are queue capacity, backpressure when full, shutdown ordering and which thread runs a task's completion.

thread-local storage (C): Objects with thread storage duration, declared thread_local (C23) or _Thread_local (C11), of which each thread has its own instance created when the thread starts and destroyed when it ends; the ELF TLS segment is the toolchain mechanism that implements it.

sets.title: T29 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Without the glossary, define exception (Arm), interrupt (Arm), interrupt handler, NVIC, Thread mode, Handler mode and exception priority, and say which document defines each.
checklist: cache maintenance: The explicit clean (write back) and invalidate operations a Cortex-M7 program must issue on the data cache around DMA transfers and shared-memory handoffs, because the cache is not coherent with bus masters or the other core; done per cache line, which makes buffer alignment part of the contract.

DMA descriptor: A memory record in a hardware-defined format that tells a bus-master controller (DMA, Ethernet MAC) where a buffer is, how long it is and who owns it; the controller and the software hand ownership back and forth through a flag in the descriptor

DMA transfer: A data movement performed by a direct-memory-access controller acting as a bus master independently of the processor; while it is in flight the processor must not touch the buffer, and on processors with data caches the buffer must be cleaned or invalidated at the right moments.
exception (Arm): Any event on an Armv7-M processor that changes the flow of execution to a handler through the vector table: reset, NMI, faults, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick and the external interrupts

exception entry and return: The hardware sequence that stacks r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR (plus floating-point registers when lazy stacking is not used), loads lr with an EXC_RETURN value encoding the stack and mode to resume, and restores the frame when the handler returns through that value.

exception priority: The number, lower meaning more urgent, that decides whether a pending exception preempts the running one; only the implemented high-order bits of the priority field matter, and reset, NMI and HardFault have fixed negative priorities above all configurable ones.
Handler mode: The processor mode entered when an exception is taken; it is always privileged and always uses the main stack pointer, and the IPSR holds the active exception number.

HardFault: The fault exception with the highest configurable precedence, taken when a fault cannot be handled by its own handler or that handler is disabled; the fault status registers (HFSR, CFSR, BFAR, MMFAR) record why, and decoding them is the first step of any fault diagnosis.

interrupt (Arm): An exception requested by a peripheral or software through the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller, numbered from 16 upward in the vector table, with a programmable priority that decides preemption among active handlers.

interrupt handler: The function whose address sits in the vector table entry for an interrupt and that the processor enters in Handler mode, with the AAPCS caller-saved registers stacked by hardware; written as an ordinary C function

interrupt latency: The time from the interrupt request being asserted to the first instruction of its handler; it includes the hardware stacking cycles, any time the interrupt is masked (PRIMASK, BASEPRI, FAULTMASK) and any higher-priority handler already running
interrupt masking: Temporarily preventing exception entry: PRIMASK blocks all configurable exceptions, BASEPRI blocks those at or below a priority, FAULTMASK blocks everything but NMI
late arrival: The behavior by which a higher-priority exception arriving while the processor is still stacking for a lower-priority one is taken first, reusing the stacking already done.

main and process stack pointers: The two banked stack pointers of Armv7-M: the main stack pointer used by handlers and by Thread mode at reset, and the process stack pointer an operating system gives to threads so that handler stacking never overruns a thread's stack

NVIC: The Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller: the processor block that holds per-interrupt enable, pending and priority registers, arbitrates among pending interrupts, and performs nesting according to priority; configured through its memory-mapped registers or the CMSIS NVIC_* functions.

PendSV: A software-triggered, lowest-priority exception that runs after all other handlers have finished; the conventional place for an RTOS context switch because it never interrupts another handler.

preemption priority: The group of priority bits, selected by the priority grouping field, that decides whether one exception can preempt another; the remaining bits form the subpriority, which only orders exceptions that are pending simultaneously and never causes preemption.

read-modify-write hazard: The loss of an update when two contexts (a handler and the foreground, or two cores) each read a register or variable, modify a bit and write it back, so the later write discards the earlier change; set/clear registers, atomic operations or masking remove it.

SVCall: The supervisor-call exception raised synchronously by the SVC instruction, used by an operating system as the entry from unprivileged Thread mode into privileged service code; its immediate value selects the service.
SysTick: The 24-bit down-counting timer inside the processor that raises the SysTick exception on reload; the usual source of the scheduler tick, independent of any vendor peripheral timer.

tail-chaining: The optimization by which the processor enters a pending exception directly from the returning handler without unstacking and restacking the frame, shortening back-to-back handler latency.

Thread mode: The processor mode in which application code runs, entered at reset and on return from the last active exception; it can use either stack pointer and may be privileged or unprivileged according to the CONTROL register.

vector table: The array of handler addresses, beginning with the initial main stack pointer value and the reset handler, that the processor indexes by exception number; its location is set by the VTOR register and is the first thing a startup file or linker script must place correctly.

exception entry and return: The hardware sequence that stacks r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR (plus floating-point registers when lazy stacking is not used), loads lr with an EXC_RETURN value encoding the stack and mode to resume, and restores the frame when the handler returns through that value.

exception priority: The number, lower meaning more urgent, that decides whether a pending exception preempts the running one; only the implemented high-order bits of the priority field matter, and reset, NMI and HardFault have fixed negative priorities above all configurable ones.
Handler mode: The processor mode entered when an exception is taken; it is always privileged and always uses the main stack pointer, and the IPSR holds the active exception number.

HardFault: The fault exception with the highest configurable precedence, taken when a fault cannot be handled by its own handler or that handler is disabled; the fault status registers (HFSR, CFSR, BFAR, MMFAR) record why, and decoding them is the first step of any fault diagnosis.

interrupt (Arm): An exception requested by a peripheral or software through the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller, numbered from 16 upward in the vector table, with a programmable priority that decides preemption among active handlers.

interrupt handler: The function whose address sits in the vector table entry for an interrupt and that the processor enters in Handler mode, with the AAPCS caller-saved registers stacked by hardware; written as an ordinary C function

interrupt latency: The time from the interrupt request being asserted to the first instruction of its handler; it includes the hardware stacking cycles, any time the interrupt is masked (PRIMASK, BASEPRI, FAULTMASK) and any higher-priority handler already running
interrupt masking: Temporarily preventing exception entry: PRIMASK blocks all configurable exceptions, BASEPRI blocks those at or below a priority, FAULTMASK blocks everything but NMI
late arrival: The behavior by which a higher-priority exception arriving while the processor is still stacking for a lower-priority one is taken first, reusing the stacking already done.

main and process stack pointers: The two banked stack pointers of Armv7-M: the main stack pointer used by handlers and by Thread mode at reset, and the process stack pointer an operating system gives to threads so that handler stacking never overruns a thread's stack

NVIC: The Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller: the processor block that holds per-interrupt enable, pending and priority registers, arbitrates among pending interrupts, and performs nesting according to priority; configured through its memory-mapped registers or the CMSIS NVIC_* functions.

PendSV: A software-triggered, lowest-priority exception that runs after all other handlers have finished; the conventional place for an RTOS context switch because it never interrupts another handler.

preemption priority: The group of priority bits, selected by the priority grouping field, that decides whether one exception can preempt another; the remaining bits form the subpriority, which only orders exceptions that are pending simultaneously and never causes preemption.

read-modify-write hazard: The loss of an update when two contexts (a handler and the foreground, or two cores) each read a register or variable, modify a bit and write it back, so the later write discards the earlier change; set/clear registers, atomic operations or masking remove it.

SVCall: The supervisor-call exception raised synchronously by the SVC instruction, used by an operating system as the entry from unprivileged Thread mode into privileged service code; its immediate value selects the service.
SysTick: The 24-bit down-counting timer inside the processor that raises the SysTick exception on reload; the usual source of the scheduler tick, independent of any vendor peripheral timer.

tail-chaining: The optimization by which the processor enters a pending exception directly from the returning handler without unstacking and restacking the frame, shortening back-to-back handler latency.

Thread mode: The processor mode in which application code runs, entered at reset and on return from the last active exception; it can use either stack pointer and may be privileged or unprivileged according to the CONTROL register.

vector table: The array of handler addresses, beginning with the initial main stack pointer value and the reset handler, that the processor indexes by exception number; its location is set by the VTOR register and is the first thing a startup file or linker script must place correctly.

sets.title: T30 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define release time, response time, jitter, worst-case execution time, period and deadline without the glossary and name the source for each.
checklist: context switch: Saving the running task's registers and stack pointer and restoring another task's, on Cortex-M split between the hardware exception frame and the software-saved callee registers in PendSV; its cost and its interaction with the floating-point context are measurable dispatch overheads.

cooperative scheduler: A scheduler in which a task runs until it yields or blocks; switches happen only at known points, which removes most data races between tasks but makes response time depend on the longest run between yields.
deadline: The latest acceptable completion time of a job relative to its release; a hard deadline makes a late result worthless or dangerous, a soft one degrades value

jitter: The variation of a timing quantity (release, start or completion) between successive jobs relative to the ideal periodic instants; it is a distribution, reported with its maximum and its source, not a single number.
measured maximum: The largest value of a timing quantity observed in a recorded campaign, reported with its inputs, clock, build identity and uncertainty; evidence about that campaign only.

period: The fixed interval between successive releases of a periodic task; the deadline is often but not necessarily equal to it, and the period, not the execution time, determines how much processor time the task demands.

preemptive scheduler: A scheduler that can suspend the running task at any instruction boundary in favor of a higher-priority ready task, usually from a tick or interrupt handler through PendSV on Cortex-M; every shared datum then needs explicit synchronization.

release time: The instant at which a job of a periodic or event-driven task becomes ready to run; the reference point from which latency and response time are measured, which a timer-driven system must record independently of when the job actually starts.

response time: The interval from a job's release to its completion, including waiting for higher-priority work and its own execution; the quantity compared against the deadline in response-time analysis.

stack depth analysis: Establishing the maximum stack use of a task from the call graph and per-function frame sizes (compiler -fstack-usage reports) plus interrupt nesting, rather than from a fill-pattern high-water mark observed in testing.

superloop: The simplest firmware structure: one infinite loop that polls inputs and runs each activity in turn, with interrupts only setting flags; its response time is bounded by the sum of all activities, which is why it stops scaling.

tick: The periodic timer interrupt that advances the scheduler's notion of time and drives time slicing and delays; tick resolution bounds the precision of timeouts, and a tickless mode suppresses ticks during idle to save power at the cost of wakeup bookkeeping.

timer wraparound: The return of a free-running counter to zero after its maximum; comparisons of absolute timestamps break at the wrap, while unsigned differences modulo the counter width remain correct as long as intervals are shorter than half the range.

wakeup race: The lost-wakeup hazard in which a task checks for pending work, finds none, and enters a low-power wait after the interrupt that would have woken it has already fired; closed by checking the condition with interrupts masked and using an instruction (WFE/WFI) that honors events that arrived during the check.

watchdog: A hardware timer that resets the device unless software refreshes it within a window; it bounds the time the system can stay unresponsive, not the correctness of what it does, and a refresh placed in a timer handler defeats it.

worst-case execution time: An upper bound on the execution time of a code path over all inputs and hardware states, established by analysis or exhaustive argument; a measured maximum is a lower bound on it and never a substitute

sets.title: T44 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define symptom, first divergence, minimal reproducer, invariant, bisection and core dump without the glossary and name the reading that defines each.
checklist: backtrace: The chain of stack frames from the current function to the entry point, reconstructed from frame pointers or unwind tables; a corrupted stack or omitted frame pointers produce a misleading backtrace, which is itself a symptom.

bisection: Binary search over an ordered set of candidates (commits, inputs, build flags, code regions) for the first one that exhibits the symptom; git bisect automates it over history, and the same idea reduces inputs and configurations.

breakpoint: A debugger-inserted stop at a code address (software breakpoint, by patching an instruction) or on an address match in a hardware comparator; stopping changes timing, which matters for interrupt-driven and concurrent code.

cause: The earliest invalid state transition in the execution history that, had it not occurred, would have prevented the symptom; established by observation and a discriminating test, never by the symptom alone.

competing hypothesis: An alternative explanation of the symptom that fits the same evidence; a discriminating test is an observation or experiment whose outcome differs under the two hypotheses, and diagnosis proceeds by eliminating hypotheses, not by confirming the favorite.

core dump: The kernel's snapshot of a process's memory and registers at abnormal termination, written when the RLIMIT_CORE limit and core_pattern allow; loaded into GDB it shows the stopped state, which is evidence about the end of the history, not the history itself.

deterministic replay: Re-executing a failure with recorded inputs, schedules and timing so that it recurs on demand; a replay establishes causality where a repeated stress run only establishes frequency.

fault status decoding: Reading the Cortex-M fault status registers (CFSR with its memory-management, bus and usage subfields, HFSR, BFAR, MMFAR) and the stacked frame to establish which access faulted, why and from where; the first evidence after any HardFault.

first divergence: The earliest point at which an execution's observed state differs from the independently predicted state; locating it, rather than the point of failure, is the goal of stepping, logging and watchpoints.

invariant: A property of program state that must hold at specified points (between operations on a data structure, at loop heads); checking invariants converts a vague symptom into the first operation that broke one, and repairing the invariant, not the symptom, is the fix.

minimal reproducer: The smallest input, configuration and program fragment that still produces the symptom, obtained by systematic reduction (delta debugging); it is the artifact that makes a defect reportable, bisectable and testable.
optimized out: A variable or frame the debugger cannot show because optimization eliminated or relocated it; the program is correct, the debug information is incomplete

regression test: The minimal reproducer turned into a permanent automated check that fails if the defect returns; the last step of every diagnosis, and the evidence that the repair addressed the cause rather than the symptom.

sanitizer: Compiler instrumentation (AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer) that checks memory accesses, undefined operations or data races at run time and reports the first violation with a stack trace; it observes only executed paths and changes layout and timing.

symptom: The observable deviation from the contract (a wrong output, a signal, a hang, a timing miss) that starts a diagnosis; it is evidence about the failure's effect, not its cause, and the same symptom can arise from many causes.

watchpoint: A stop triggered by a read or write of a memory location, implemented by hardware comparators (DWT on Cortex-M, debug registers on x86) or, far more slowly, by single-stepping; the tool for finding who corrupts a variable.

sets.title: T45 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define heap corruption, double free, stack exhaustion, off-by-one error, allocation failure and asynchronous lifetime without the glossary and name the source behind each.
checklist: AddressSanitizer: Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) that surrounds allocations with redzones and tracks freed memory in quarantine so that out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free, double free and some stack errors abort with a diagnosed stack trace; it observes only executed paths and roughly doubles memory and time.

allocation failure: A null pointer returned by malloc, calloc or realloc because the request cannot be satisfied; code that assumes success dereferences a null pointer, and code that writes p = realloc(p, n) loses the original block on failure.

asynchronous lifetime: An object whose lifetime must outlast the function that created it because a DMA controller, a completion callback or another thread still refers to it; freeing or reusing it before the asynchronous consumer finishes is a use-after-free that no single-threaded test shows.
double free: Passing the same pointer to free twice without an intervening allocation of the same address; the behavior is undefined, and allocators may silently corrupt their free lists or abort

fault injection: Deliberately making an allocation, I/O or backend operation fail at a scheduled point to exercise the error path; a memory-failure drill injects allocation failure and truncation and checks that invariants, cleanup and reporting survive.

fixed-region collision: Overlap between statically placed regions of a firmware image (stack, heap, .data, .bss, retained sections) caused by a linker-script or startup error, so that one region's growth silently overwrites another; detected by linker assertions, map-file inspection and fill-pattern checks, not by tests alone.

generation-checked handle: A handle that pairs a slot index with a generation counter incremented on every release of the slot, so that a stale handle to a reused slot is rejected instead of aliasing the new occupant; the curriculum's standard defense against stale-identity reuse in pools.

heap corruption: Damage to the allocator's own bookkeeping (chunk headers, free lists) or to a neighboring allocation caused by an out-of-bounds write, a double free or an invalid free; the symptom usually appears later, inside malloc or free, far from the cause.

invalid free: Calling free on a pointer that did not come from malloc, calloc, realloc or aligned_alloc, such as an interior pointer, a stack address or a pointer from another allocator; undefined behavior that typically corrupts the heap.

Memcheck: Valgrind's default tool, which runs an uninstrumented binary under dynamic translation and tracks definedness bit by bit, reporting uninitialized reads, invalid accesses, invalid frees and leaks at a large slowdown; complementary to AddressSanitizer rather than redundant with it.

null-termination defect: A buffer treated as a string although no null character lies within its bounds, often after strncpy filled it completely or a length-limited read stopped early; every subsequent str* call reads out of bounds.

off-by-one error: A bound computed one element too far or too short, typically from confusing a count with the last valid index or forgetting the terminating null character; the most common source of a one-byte out-of-bounds write.

resize invalidation: The invalidation of every pointer into a block when realloc moves it; the old pointers become dangling even though the bytes were copied, and the old block must not be freed or used.
retention: Storage that is still reachable and still allocated but no longer needed, such as a cache that never evicts; unlike a memory leak it can be released, yet it exhausts memory just the same.

stack corruption: Overwriting data in a stack frame (saved return address, saved registers, neighboring locals) through an out-of-bounds write into an automatic array; the stack protector detects the sequential case, the symptom is often a return to a wrong address.

stack exhaustion: Running out of stack space through deep recursion, large automatic arrays or a too-small configured stack; on Linux it ends in SIGSEGV on the guard page, on a Cortex-M it overruns into whatever lies below the stack unless an MPU guard or stack limit register catches it.

stack corruption: Overwriting data in a stack frame (saved return address, saved registers, neighboring locals) through an out-of-bounds write into an automatic array; the stack protector detects the sequential case, the symptom is often a return to a wrong address.

stack exhaustion: Running out of stack space through deep recursion, large automatic arrays or a too-small configured stack; on Linux it ends in SIGSEGV on the guard page, on a Cortex-M it overruns into whatever lies below the stack unless an MPU guard or stack limit register catches it.

checklist: AddressSanitizer: Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) that surrounds allocations with redzones and tracks freed memory in quarantine so that out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free, double free and some stack errors abort with a diagnosed stack trace; it observes only executed paths and roughly doubles memory and time.

allocation failure: A null pointer returned by malloc, calloc or realloc because the request cannot be satisfied; code that assumes success dereferences a null pointer, and code that writes p = realloc(p, n) loses the original block on failure.

asynchronous lifetime: An object whose lifetime must outlast the function that created it because a DMA controller, a completion callback or another thread still refers to it; freeing or reusing it before the asynchronous consumer finishes is a use-after-free that no single-threaded test shows.
double free: Passing the same pointer to free twice without an intervening allocation of the same address; the behavior is undefined, and allocators may silently corrupt their free lists or abort

fault injection: Deliberately making an allocation, I/O or backend operation fail at a scheduled point to exercise the error path; a memory-failure drill injects allocation failure and truncation and checks that invariants, cleanup and reporting survive.

fixed-region collision: Overlap between statically placed regions of a firmware image (stack, heap, .data, .bss, retained sections) caused by a linker-script or startup error, so that one region's growth silently overwrites another; detected by linker assertions, map-file inspection and fill-pattern checks, not by tests alone.

generation-checked handle: A handle that pairs a slot index with a generation counter incremented on every release of the slot, so that a stale handle to a reused slot is rejected instead of aliasing the new occupant; the curriculum's standard defense against stale-identity reuse in pools.

heap corruption: Damage to the allocator's own bookkeeping (chunk headers, free lists) or to a neighboring allocation caused by an out-of-bounds write, a double free or an invalid free; the symptom usually appears later, inside malloc or free, far from the cause.

invalid free: Calling free on a pointer that did not come from malloc, calloc, realloc or aligned_alloc, such as an interior pointer, a stack address or a pointer from another allocator; undefined behavior that typically corrupts the heap.

Memcheck: Valgrind's default tool, which runs an uninstrumented binary under dynamic translation and tracks definedness bit by bit, reporting uninitialized reads, invalid accesses, invalid frees and leaks at a large slowdown; complementary to AddressSanitizer rather than redundant with it.

null-termination defect: A buffer treated as a string although no null character lies within its bounds, often after strncpy filled it completely or a length-limited read stopped early; every subsequent str* call reads out of bounds.

off-by-one error: A bound computed one element too far or too short, typically from confusing a count with the last valid index or forgetting the terminating null character; the most common source of a one-byte out-of-bounds write.

variants.prompt: Define durable commit, redo log, checkpoint, torn write and crash consistency without the glossary and name the source for each.
checklist: checkpoint: A recorded point in the log at which all page updates before it have been made durable, so recovery may start replay there instead of at the beginning; it bounds recovery time and permits log truncation.

crash consistency: The property that after a crash at any instant the recovered store is a prefix of the committed history (no committed transaction lost, no uncommitted effect visible); achieved by write ordering, durable commit points and recovery, and tested by injecting crashes at every write boundary.

durable commit: The point at which a store guarantees that a committed transaction's effects will survive a crash: its log records have reached stable storage (fsync or fdatasync completed) in an order that recovery can replay

idempotent redo: The property that applying a log record to a page that already reflects it changes nothing, obtained by recording the page's log sequence number and skipping older records; it lets recovery replay from a checkpoint without knowing exactly where the crash struck.

page format: The byte-exact layout of a store page: header with type, identity and log sequence number, slot directory or records, and a checksum or trailer that reveals a torn write; it is a contract independent of the host's struct layout and endianness.

recovery: The procedure run at startup after an unclean shutdown that analyzes the log from the last checkpoint, redoes committed changes missing from the pages and undoes or ignores uncommitted ones, leaving a crash-consistent store before any client is served.

redo log: An append-only sequence of records describing changes to pages, written and made durable before the pages themselves (write-ahead), so that recovery can reapply changes that reached the log but not the data pages

torn write: A multi-sector page write of which only part reached the device before a crash, leaving a page that is neither the old nor the new contents; detected by a per-page checksum or a trailer that must match the header, and the reason page formats carry one.

variants.prompt: For Linux kernel programming and lifetime boundaries, define module init unwind, publication boundary (module), user-copy residual, staged kernel publication, reference handoff (kernel), reference resurrection, raw spin context, CPU-local exclusion, work quiescence, admission closure, retirement (RCU model), reader grace obligation, kernel wire ABI, compatibility admission, module text lifetime, detached device owner, giving each invariant.
checklist: admission closure: Transition that prevents new work from extending a closing lifecycle.
compatibility admission: Decision to accept a message version before interpreting its fields.
CPU-local exclusion: Prevention of selected concurrent execution on one processor.
detached device owner: Open reference whose device has been removed but whose cleanup still must run.
kernel wire ABI: Explicit byte-level contract for a userspace/kernel control record.
module init unwind: Reverse release of resources owned by a partially initialized module.
module text lifetime: Interval in which stored callbacks may legally execute module code.
publication boundary (module): The first point at which another context can find module-owned state.
raw spin context: Execution region governed by a strict spinning kernel lock.
reader grace obligation: Requirement that all relevant pre-removal read sections finish before reclaiming storage.
reference handoff (kernel): Transfer or acquisition of a counted lifetime claim before asynchronous publication.
reference resurrection: Attempt to reacquire ownership after terminal lifetime release.
retirement (RCU model): Removal of a published object while retaining storage for prior readers.
staged kernel publication: Private validation before a new record becomes reachable.
user-copy residual: Count of bytes a kernel user-copy operation did not transfer.
work quiescence: State in which no pending or running worker can access the owned object.

strong reference: An owned participation in the shared value lifetime that prevents destruction while it remains live.

weak reference: A reference that retains the shared control metadata but requires successful upgrade before accessing a live value.

variants.prompt: Define receiver/table association, invocation capability, authority attenuation and loaded-code borrow.
checklist: authority attenuation: Delegation that grants only a subset of the source authority under an enforcing boundary.
capture environment: Stored or borrowed values on which a closure body depends in addition to its explicit arguments.
closure invocation capability: The access mode needed to invoke a closure: shared observation, mutation or consumption of its environment.
dispatch cache epoch: A version included in cached method decisions so mutations of the method universe can invalidate prior hits and misses.
embedded operation table pointer: Dispatch metadata stored within each concrete owner rather than only in an external view.
erased callable owner: A callable wrapper responsible for capture storage and explicit destruction/movement under its contract.
erased interface view: Borrowed access to a concrete receiver together with operations that can act on it without exposing its type to the consumer.
initial-member recovery: Conversion of a pointer to an actual initial struct member back to its live containing struct under the first-member rule.
intrusive membership: Participation in a container through link storage embedded in the participating object.
invocation thunk: An adapter that reconstructs the concrete call contract behind an erased callable signature.
loaded-code borrow: An outstanding right to use a loaded module API or callback while its code/data owner remains loaded.
nominal interface registration: An explicit association between a named concrete type and a named interface implementation.
opaque module lease: A live factory-issued reference whose hidden state may be used until its explicit close operation.
operation dictionary: An explicit collection of functions supplied as evidence of supported operations to a generic algorithm.
ordered dispatch key: A tuple of dynamic argument identities whose order selects a registered operation.
receiver/table association: The invariant that each erased object is interpreted only by operations for its actual concrete representation.
reload quiescence: A declared state in which no admitted user can still invoke or access code/data scheduled for retirement.
retired module owner: Explicit retained ownership of an old module after a new one is committed and before cleanup completes.

variants.prompt: Define inline capacity, persistent collection version, bitmap child rank and rope concatenation node from their invariants.
checklist: archetype migration: Transfer of an entity between component-set tables with both table and entity mappings repaired.
archetype table: Rows of entities with the same component-set mask and typed per-component columns.
bitmap child rank: The count of occupied logical child slots preceding a selected slot, used as a compact-array index.
dense/rank inverse: Two index arrays whose compositions recover each live slot ID and each live dense position.
full-hash collision: Distinct admitted keys having the same complete hash value and therefore requiring a separate equality test.
hot column: A parallel field array visited by the selected common operation, whose hotness is relative to that workload.
inline capacity: The number of live elements representable within the container owner before requesting separate storage.
lane saturation: Clamping each independently computed lane result at its representable maximum before packing.
packed arithmetic lane: A fixed bit-field within an unsigned word treated as an independent numeric operand by a proved operation.
path copying: Constructing fresh nodes on a changed root-to-focus path while sharing untouched subtrees with older roots.
persistent collection version: An observable root whose logical value remains available after creation of another version sharing its unchanged nodes.
retained root set: The externally held version roots whose reachable nodes must remain live under the reclamation contract.
rope balance bound: A declared relation between depth and represented length used to detect excessive traversal height.
rope concatenation node: An ordered pair of text-subsequence roots with a cached combined logical length.
segmented element storage: Payload arrays in separate stable pages addressed through a movable page index.
small-buffer owner: An object that selects inline or separately owned storage according to its capacity/lifetime protocol.
spill transition: A container state change from owner-local storage to separately allocated storage.
text coordinate domain: The chosen units of an edit position, such as bytes, decoded scalars or grapheme boundaries.

variants.prompt: Using the protocol lab representations, define typestate, staged builder completeness, a session transition, hierarchical-state least common ancestor, orthogonal region, run-to-completion and a driver capability.
checklist: abort callback: An operation that releases or cancels the resources of a still-running behavior-tree action under a specified exactly-once policy.
active object: A stateful object that owns an event queue and processes admitted events through a serialized dispatch policy.
binary session: A communication protocol between exactly two endpoints with a specified sequence of complementary actions.
consuming transition: A protocol operation that invalidates one admitted token and produces a token for the resulting state, or retains a separate recovery obligation.
external self transition: A transition whose source and target are the same state but which still executes that state’s exit and entry actions.
hierarchical state machine: A state machine whose nested active states share event handling and whose transitions have defined ancestor-based entry and exit behavior.
internal transition: An event reaction that does not exit and reenter the active state.
memory behavior tree: A behavior tree whose composites remember the child at which execution suspended and skip earlier completed children on the next tick.
presence mask: A bitset recording which required fields have been supplied, separately from whether their values are valid together.
recovery-required state: A state recording that partial effects prevent nominal reuse until an explicit recovery operation establishes its postcondition.
run-to-completion step: A dispatch interval during which one admitted event is handled before another event begins dispatch on the same machine.
running leaf: A behavior-tree leaf whose action has started but has not yet returned a terminal outcome.
session duality: The relation obtained by exchanging send and receive actions while preserving the corresponding protocol progression.
stackless protothread: A resumable function that stores its continuation label and persistent data explicitly instead of retaining its native call stack.
staged builder: An interface that exposes different construction operations according to which configuration stage has been reached.
typestate token: A wrapper identifying the currently admitted operations on a live object; this C model checks its generation at runtime.

variants.prompt: Using the coroutine representations, define a suspended frame, continuation, defunctionalized tag, yield boundary, fiber stack, parser commitment, packrat memo entry and exactly-once completion.
checklist: coroutine frame: Storage holding the control state and variables that must remain live across suspension.
defunctionalization: Replacing a finite family of continuation functions with tagged data describing their environments and a dispatcher interpreting those tags.
fiber fake stack: Sanitizer-managed storage that may hold locals for use-after-return detection independently of the architectural stack pointer.
generator suspension: A point at which a generator returns a value or pending status while retaining the state needed for later progress.
internal iteration: Iteration in which an operation drives traversal and invokes a consumer callback, including an explicitly typed early-exit policy.
iterator fusion: Combining iterator stages while preserving their value, consumption, evaluation and failure contracts.
nullable repetition: Repetition of a parser that can succeed without consuming input, requiring an explicit policy to prevent nonprogress.
ordered choice: A parsing operation that selects the first successful alternative and retries later alternatives only under its declared mismatch policy.
packrat memoization: Caching parsing results by rule and input position together with every other semantic dependency admitted by the cache contract.
parser combinator: An operation that constructs a parser by composing smaller parsers under declared consumption and failure semantics.
pull iterator: An interface in which the consumer requests each next value, allowing demand to control producer progress.
single-shot continuation: A resumable control-and-environment value whose contract permits at most one successful consumption.
stackful fiber: A cooperative execution context with its own retained call stack and an explicitly specified context-switch ABI.
trampoline: An iterative dispatcher that advances explicit continuation states without requiring one native recursive call per logical step.
Volcano operator: A query-processing operator with an open/next/close interface that produces values on downstream demand.

variants.prompt: Define nursery, incarnation, read version, snapshot pin and demand credit with exact lifetime events.
checklist: actor incarnation: One lifetime of an actor identified separately from its reusable storage address.
commit validation: Checking a transaction’s read dependencies while holding its write locks before publishing staged values.
cooperative checkpoint: A point where a task observes cancellation and may return through its normal cleanup path.
demand credit: The admitted number of future item signals, with an explicit sentinel for unbounded demand.
last-item arbitration: The atomic winner selection between owner and thief for the final deque entry.
operation completion ownership: The right to release connected operation storage at its terminal callback under the declared backend protocol.
rendezvous acknowledgment: The receiver transition that completes a zero-capacity channel send after accepting its offered value.
restart dependency order: The reverse-stop and forward-start sequence that preserves the declared child dependencies.
restart intensity: A bounded count of admitted restart-triggering failures within a stated time window.
selection registration: The protocol connecting readiness inspection to waiter notification without an unprotected lost-wakeup interval.
sequence validation: Accepting atomic payload reads only between matching even sequence observations under the stated ordering and no-wrap assumptions.
snapshot pin: A generation-tagged reader record that retains the version visible at its captured timestamp.
task nursery: A scope that owns admitted child tasks and retains their borrowed contexts until every child is joined.
terminal signal: The single final success or error notification after which this stream admits no item signals.
transaction read version: The snapshot timestamp that bounds versions a transaction may admit when reading shared cells.
visible-version retention: Keeping exactly the current version and versions selected by live snapshot readers under this finite-store contract.

commit validation: Checking a transaction’s read dependencies while holding its write locks before publishing staged values.
cooperative checkpoint: A point where a task observes cancellation and may return through its normal cleanup path.
demand credit: The admitted number of future item signals, with an explicit sentinel for unbounded demand.
last-item arbitration: The atomic winner selection between owner and thief for the final deque entry.
operation completion ownership: The right to release connected operation storage at its terminal callback under the declared backend protocol.
rendezvous acknowledgment: The receiver transition that completes a zero-capacity channel send after accepting its offered value.
restart dependency order: The reverse-stop and forward-start sequence that preserves the declared child dependencies.
restart intensity: A bounded count of admitted restart-triggering failures within a stated time window.
selection registration: The protocol connecting readiness inspection to waiter notification without an unprotected lost-wakeup interval.
sequence validation: Accepting atomic payload reads only between matching even sequence observations under the stated ordering and no-wrap assumptions.
snapshot pin: A generation-tagged reader record that retains the version visible at its captured timestamp.
task nursery: A scope that owns admitted child tasks and retains their borrowed contexts until every child is joined.
terminal signal: The single final success or error notification after which this stream admits no item signals.
transaction read version: The snapshot timestamp that bounds versions a transaction may admit when reading shared cells.
visible-version retention: Keeping exactly the current version and versions selected by live snapshot readers under this finite-store contract.

sets.title: T74 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define selected runtime terms with their invariants.
checklist: card marking: Recording potentially relevant writes at a coarser storage-region granularity, allowing conservative rescanning.
derived reference: A reference described by an allocation base and an offset, so relocation can preserve its relation to the allocation.
ephemeron: A conditional association whose value becomes reachable only when its key is independently reachable.
finalization resurrection: Making an object reachable again while processing a finalizer, requiring a defined later-reclamation policy.
forwarding address: A record connecting an object old location to its new location so aliases can be rewritten consistently.
hidden class: An immutable descriptor identity representing an object property layout, distinct from the set of property names alone.
monomorphic inline cache: A lookup-site cache specialized to one guarded receiver layout and operation.
NaN boxing: A value encoding that reserves selected floating-point NaN bit patterns for other tags and payloads under explicit representation assumptions.
polymorphic inline cache: A bounded list of guarded receiver-layout handlers used before a generic lookup fallback.
precise root map: Metadata identifying exactly the live reference-bearing locations at a permitted collection point.
promotion: Moving a surviving young-generation object into an older generation under an explicit policy.
remembered set: Metadata recording references across a collection boundary so omitted regions need not be fully traced.
safepoint: A designated execution state at which the runtime can enumerate and, where supported, update all live references required by collection.
semispace: One of two regions whose source and destination roles alternate during copying collection.
shape transition: A mapping from an existing layout and structural mutation to the resulting layout identity.
string interning: Canonicalizing equal byte sequences into a shared identity whose lifetime and retention belong to an owning table.
tagged pointer: An integer representation carrying a tag that must be removed under a documented pointer-mapping contract before recovering a live pointer.
tri-color invariant: A collector invariant preventing scanned black objects from acquiring unrecorded references to unmarked white objects.
trial deletion: Computing candidate external reference counts and reachability using temporary counts before deciding which cycles are collectible.
write barrier: An operation coupled to mutation that preserves a collector invariant or records references requiring later processing.

sets.title: T75 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define deadline, remaining budget, retry budget, fencing and quiescence.
checklist: backpressure: A protocol that makes producer progress depend on consumer capacity rather than allowing unconstrained outstanding work.
bulkhead: An admission boundary that limits simultaneous retained resource ownership, optionally reserving capacity between tenants.
burst credit: Stored token capacity that permits a bounded admission burst beyond the replenishment rate over a short interval.
cancellation acknowledgement: Evidence that a previously admitted operation has reached a terminal state and released its borrowing obligations.
committed notification outbox: Owned notification state reserved or durably recorded alongside an effect so later delivery has an explicit recovery path.
deduplication window: The explicitly bounded retention interval in which a request identity maps to its original effect and result.
fencing token: A monotonically ordered authority marker checked by the protected resource to reject writes from older owners.
flow credit: An explicit permission to consume a bounded amount of receiver capacity, conserved across admission and release.
half-open probe: A bounded admission used to test recovery after a circuit breaker open period.
hedged request: An additional overlapping attempt intended to obtain an acceptable response sooner while retaining ownership of every started attempt.
lazy refill: Computing accumulated resource credit at an observed time rather than updating it on every clock tick.
operation quiescence: The state in which every started operation has terminated its access to the resources proposed for reclamation.
overload policy: The declared behavior when offered work exceeds available admission capacity.
remaining budget: A duration still available after accounting for elapsed work and declared propagation costs.
request deadline: A time bound in a specified clock domain after which a request no longer admits waiting or work under its contract.
retry budget: A limit on extra attempts or resources spent after an original request fails or becomes uncertain.
retry jitter: Variation in retry scheduling intended to reduce correlated simultaneous demand under a stated randomization model.
timer cascade: Movement of a coarse timer into a finer timing level as its expiry approaches.
timer-wheel bucket: A group of candidate timers selected by a modular time index; a full expiry discriminator distinguishes different revolutions.

sets.title: T76 vocabulary

variants.prompt: Define every representation and validity condition in this domain using its actual C declarations.
checklist: anti-entropy range commitment: A hash tied to an exact ordered range and tree shape used to locate divergence.
canonical field-map encoding: One byte sequence selected by explicit ordering, numeric and duplicate rules for a semantic field map.
causal delta interval: A joined range of deltas whose receiver must satisfy the required predecessor-state condition.
effect request value: Data describing an intended external action returned by a pure transition.
event position: A stable ordinal within one identified immutable log history.
happened-before order: The transitive relation generated by local event order and message send-before-receive.
HLC physical maximum: The largest physical component known through local wall observations and received histories.
Merkle domain separation: Distinct input encodings for leaf and interior-node hash computations.
minimal varint: The shortest base128 continuation encoding of an admitted unsigned integer.
observed removal: Removal of the particular add identities visible to a replica.
projection application identity: The combination of log identity, event position and immutable event content used to admit a duplicate.
projection commit boundary: The atomic transition joining query-state change and its progress cursor.
projection snapshot root: A retained immutable root describing state after a particular event prefix.
register arbitration stamp: A protocol-defined totally ordered event identity selecting a value.
replay state completeness: The snapshot contains every value that can influence future core transitions under recorded inputs.
sequence anchor identity: A persistent node identifier used to locate insertion context after visible edits.
state join idempotence: Joining an admitted state with itself leaves it unchanged.
transformation context: The document version and causal history relative to which an operation was defined.
